evidence.label: A dimension-free logarithmic Sobolev inequality for subgaussian log-concave measures

headline: Log-concave laws with bell-curve tails in every direction obey a dimension-free log-Sobolev bound, the paper claims.
scope: The result covers centered log-concave probability laws with a density on n-dimensional space, whose linear projections all have bell-curve tails with a common scale a.
plain: A logarithmic Sobolev inequality bounds how uneven a function can be by how steep it is on average. The question is whether bell-curve tails in every straight direction are enough to get one, for one-hump (log-concave) distributions. This paper claims they are, with constant C times a squared, where C is the same in every dimension. Earlier bounds grew with the dimension, like n or the square root of n. No Lean formalization is listed.
doesNot: This does not give a numerical value for the universal constant C, and it does not cover laws without the log-concave shape.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Pierre Bizeul, who formulated the conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a stated conjecture on log-concave laws by removing all dependence on dimension.

explanation:
Start with the bell curve, the standard normal distribution. Draw X from it and compute the average of exp(X²/a²). The answer is 1 divided by the square root of 1 − 2/a². That equals 2 exactly when a² = 8/3, so a is about 1.63. In the paper's terms, X is a-subgaussian with a ≈ 1.63. Being linearly a-subgaussian means every straight projection passes this test with the same a[13].

Now take a standard bell curve in n dimensions. Every straight projection of it is again a standard bell curve. So the same a ≈ 1.63 works in every dimension, even a million. The question is whether that kind of tail control buys something much stronger.

The stronger thing is a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. It bounds the entropy of a function [a number measuring how uneven its values are] by its Dirichlet energy [the average squared steepness][1]. It also gives bell-curve concentration for every Lipschitz function [a function that cannot change faster than a fixed rate][2]. Write the bound as entropy ≤ constant × energy. For the bell curve, a classical result of Bakry and Émery keeps the constant fixed in every dimension[3]. Their method needs the density to curve downward at a guaranteed rate.

This paper works with log-concave laws [densities whose logarithm is concave, giving one hump and light tails]. Log-concavity alone promises no guaranteed downward curvature[4]. So the classical method has nothing to push against. The question is whether bell-curve tails in every straight direction can replace that curvature[5]. The tails are necessary, up to universal constants[6]. Pierre Bizeul formulated their sufficiency as a conjecture in 2023[7].

Earlier bounds grew with dimension. A criterion of Bobkov from 1999 gives a constant of order n × a²[8]. Bizeul improved this to order √n × a²[9]. In 10,000 dimensions, those are 10,000a² and 100a². Bizeul also proved the dimension-free bound for laws that look the same in every direction[10].

The paper claims the constant is C × a², with one universal C[11]. The same C works in every dimension[12]. No smoothness of the density or positive curvature is needed[14]. So the theorem includes uniform measures on convex bodies [solid shapes with no dents][15]. The theorem names no numerical value for C. It needs the law to be centered, with average zero, and to have a density.

The hard part is the gap between hypothesis and conclusion. The tail condition speaks only about straight, linear functions. The conclusion controls the entropy of every nonlinear test function[16]. The paper argues by contradiction. A failure would give laws whose log-Sobolev constant stays at 1 while their tail scale a shrinks to zero[17]. The paper then derives two incompatible descriptions of how these laws fluctuate[18].

There is also a standard consequence. By a 2000 result of Otto and Villani, the bound implies a transport–entropy inequality with the same constant[19]. That inequality limits how far a distribution can be moved, in an average-distance sense, by its relative entropy.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. The constant C is universal but not given as a number, and the law must be centered and log-concave. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A bound on the entropy of a function by a constant times its average squared steepness.
Here, a number that measures how uneven the values of a function are under a given distribution.
A density whose logarithm is concave, so it has a single hump and light tails.
Every straight projection has tails no heavier than a bell curve of a fixed width a.
The constant stays the same no matter how many dimensions the space has.
A function that cannot change faster than a fixed rate.
A solid shape with no dents: the segment between any two of its points stays inside.

claims.text: A logarithmic Sobolev inequality controls entropy by Dirichlet energy.
claims.sourceLine: A logarithmic Sobolev inequality controls the entropy of a function by its Dirichlet energy.
claims.sourceQuote: A logarithmic Sobolev inequality controls the entropy of a function by its Dirichlet energy.

claims.text: It gives Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions.
claims.sourceLine: it gives Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions
claims.sourceQuote: Besides implying a Poincar\'e inequality, it gives Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions.

claims.sourceLine: gives the inequality for a density
claims.sourceQuote: The diffusion approach of Bakry and \'Emery \cite{BakryEmery1985} gives the inequality for a density $e^{-V}$ when $D^2V\ge\kappa\Id$ with $\kappa>0$: in the convention used below, its constant is at most $\kappa^{-1}$.

claims.text: Log-concavity alone asserts only nonnegative Hessian.
claims.sourceQuote: Log-concavity alone asserts only $D^2V\ge0$ when the potential is smooth.

claims.text: The question is whether tail assumptions on linear functions can replace positive curvature.

claims.sourceQuote: The question addressed here is whether a global assumption on the tails of linear functions can supply the logarithmic Sobolev bound without positive curvature.

claims.sourceQuote: Under \eqref{eq:intro-subgaussian}, H\"older's inequality gives $\E\exp(|X|^2/(na^2))\le2$, so that criterion yields a coefficient of order $na^2$.

claims.text: Every centered log-concave law with linear subgaussian parameter a satisfies Ent(f²) ≤ C a² ∫|Df|² with universal C.
claims.sourceQuote: We prove that every centered log-concave probability measure with a Lebesgue density on $\mathbb R^n$ and linear subgaussian parameter $a$ satisfies $\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f^2)\le Ca^2\int|Df|^2\,d\mu$ for compactly supported smooth $f$, with one universal constant $C$.
